transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Laura Kim (Pioneer CTO), Ben Torres (Pioneer ML), Amy Ross (Product), Jason Li (Infra)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, and with me is Samir our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Laura Kim: Doing well, thanks. We have about 40 minutes, we wanted a straight-forward demo of hosted API for chat and text gen — particularly streaming and retry behavior.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Perfect. We'll keep it focused. Quick agenda: 1) Hosted API basics and SDK, 2) streaming and params, 3) retry/timeout semantics and error handling, 4) Q&A and next steps.
[00:24] Samir Patel: I'll jump into the console and live demo after a couple slides, show sample snippets for Node/Python, and then we can talk about lat/cost tradeoffs and VPC/private options.

Summary & context gathering:
[00:38] Maya Chen: Laura, could you give a quick sense of your current stack and goals?
[00:42] Laura Kim: Sure. Pioneer is building a conversational insights product on top of in-house event streams. We currently run some inference on GCP using a managed endpoint but it's expensive and latency is not great during spikes. We want a hosted option initially, maybe move to dedicated later, goal is < 300ms token latency for short responses, and cost needs to be below $0.0015 per token equivalent — rough numbers.
[01:05] Ben Torres: Also we need streaming for real-time UI, and robust retry policy because some upstream calls fail during bursts. Data residency — EU region — and SOC2 compliance are must-haves.
[01:18] Maya Chen: Great notes. That aligns with the hosted API use-case we typically demo.

Topic: Hosted API overview
[01:30] Samir Patel: Ok switching to screen — here's the Redwood Console. Top-level: model catalog, per-route dashboards, and an API keys page. For hosted API you get REST endpoints and SDKs; the same API surface works across hosted, dedicated, and private with minimal config changes.
[01:52] Samir Patel: Quick code snippet — Node example: const r = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY }); r.chat.create({ model: 'rw-chat-1', messages: [...], stream: true, temperature: 0.2 }); — that stream flag flips on server-sent events / chunked streaming.
[02:10] Amy Ross: When you say stream: true, does that guarantee token-by-token UI updates?
[02:14] Samir Patel: It sends data as it's generated. Depending on the SDK you'll either get SSE events or websocket chunks. For Node/Python we expose async iterators so you can pipe updates to the UI as they arrive. Note there might be small buffering at the transport layer — browser clients sometimes group small chunks.

Topic: Streaming and UI integration
[02:40] Samir Patel: Here's a demo app on the console — basic chat with streaming. I'll type a long prompt and show how the UI updates.
[02:48] [screen typing noise]
[03:05] Samir Patel: You can see partial tokens come in. If you want lower latency per first token, we recommend smaller context windows and model variants tuned for short-turn latency. We have perf profiles in the model catalog.
[03:24] Ben Torres: What about tokenization and counting? We want predictable billing; sometimes different models count tokens slightly differently which makes cost math fuzzy.
[03:33] Maya Chen: Good point. Redwood exposes token_count metrics per request in the response metadata and in console usage dashboards so you can reconcile. We also provide suggested batching strategies to reduce per-token cost.

Topic: Params tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences)
[03:55] Samir Patel: For temperature and top_p — classic tradeoff: higher temperature for creativity, lower for deterministic answers. For classification or extraction we recommend temp ~0 to 0.2. For open-ended summaries 0.6-0.8. max_tokens controls max output and thus cost; you can include stop sequences to terminate early.
[04:18] Samir Patel: Example: r.chat.create({ messages, max_tokens: 150, temperature: 0.2, top_p: 0.9, stream: true })
[04:26] Amy Ross: Any guardrails on length? If the model runs away, will you be charged for huge outputs?
[04:30] Maya Chen: You are charged for tokens generated. We recommend setting max_tokens and using stop sequences; Redwood also supports per-route quotas and soft limits to protect budget during POCs.

Topic: Retry, idempotency, and backoff behavior
[04:45] Samir Patel: Important bit for production: Redwood's hosted API returns clear error codes and we recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter. For idempotency, include a request_id header for non-idempotent operations or use our dedupe token — for chat it's common to include session-level ids so retries don't double-insert messages.
[05:05] Samir Patel: The SDKs implement recommended retry strategies by default: 3 retries for transient 5xx, with exponential backoff; you can override. Retries are safe as long as your application includes an idempotency key for operations that mutate state.
[05:20] Ben Torres: What about partial streams and reconnects?
[05:23] Samir Patel: If a stream fails mid-response, you can either request the model to continue from the last completed message fragment (we return generation anchors), or restart the request and pass the partial output in the context so the model resumes. There is a slight risk of duplication unless you dedupe on your side. We'll share a sample reconnect pattern.

[05:46] Samir Patel: Also note region-aware routing: for EU data residency we can route to eu-west-1 endpoints and ensure logs are kept per-region.

Topic: Latency & cost tradeoffs, model variants
[06:05] Samir Patel: Here's a perf slide — model variants optimized for low-latency vs high-quality. For your <300ms token target, we can recommend a lite variant and quantization profile. If you later need higher quality for longer context we can pin a higher-capacity model.
[06:23] Laura Kim: How deterministic are performance numbers? Our spikes are a concern.
[06:28] Maya Chen: For hosted, we publish P95 latency profiles per model and you can request dedicated capacity if you want strict throughput SLAs. For POC we usually run a benchmark in your expected workload to map cost/latency curves.

[06:44] Samir Patel: Quick demo of SDK retry options — switching to code view, show config: retries: { maxAttempts: 4, backoffBaseMs: 200, jitter: true } and an example of handling 429 rate-limit responses with backoff and token-bucket smoothing on the client.

[07:05] Jason Li: Does Redwood expose server-side rate-limits per key? We need to throttle at edge.
[07:10] Samir Patel: Yes, the API returns X-RateLimit headers and we have per-key quotas you can set in console. For integration we suggest client-side rate-limiting plus server-side quotas.

[07:25] Laura Kim: Security question — you mentioned SOC2 earlier. Also encryption, KMS, and logs — do we get access to raw logs?
[07:31] Maya Chen: Hosted customers get audit logs and usage events; for raw token-level logs we offer opt-in logging for troubleshooting but by default we do not retain full request bodies beyond the retention window. We support KMS integration for Private deployments; for hosted we encrypt at rest with provider KMS and offer additional controls for enterprise tiers. We'll share the security brief with SOC2/ISO certs.

[07:55] Samir Patel: Ok moving to a little deeper sample: I'll demo a Node streaming handler that uses async iterator and incremental UI updates.
[08:03] [screen demo]
[08:20] Samir Patel: Code shows how to parse chunked SSE events, handle partial tokens, and update a UI buffer. We include a small backfill technique if the connection drops — basically request with the last confirmed token index and include conversation history.

[08:40] Ben Torres: You said the SDK gives token indexes — how accurate are those? We need to align partials with client-side transcript.
[08:46] Samir Patel: We provide token offsets and char offsets in the stream events for most models. There are occasional off-by-one issues depending on tokenization differences; that's one of the imperfect transcription scenarios, but generally it's robust enough for UI stitching.

[09:05] Amy Ross: Any examples of batching multiple short requests to improve throughput?
[09:09] Samir Patel: Yes, Redwood supports request multiplexing and batching at the runtime. For short-turn chat, batching can reduce per-token latency cost but may add small queuing latency. We recommend adaptive batching: during quiet periods batch more aggressively, during spikes fall back to immediate mode. Optimize has suggestions for batching thresholds.

[09:35] Laura Kim: On the console — can we set per-route quotas and see token-level cost breakdowns?
[09:39] Samir Patel: Yes, per-route settings, token-level cost breakdowns, and per-token latency heatmaps. You can drill down by API key, model, and timeframe.

[09:52] [10:00] Mist: filler noise, small overlap

Topic: Observability and debugging
[10:05] Samir Patel: For debugging we have trace ids on every request, plus a replay feature that can replay inputs against model variants in a sandbox. That helps with regressions after model updates. We also have evaluation hooks so you can run prompt sets and get automated quality metrics.
[10:24] Ben Torres: Can we run A/B tests with two model variants?
[10:27] Samir Patel: Absolutely — rollouts in console support canary and A/B with weighted routing. You can set automatic fallback if latency or quality drops.

Topic: Billing and pricing (brief)
[10:40] Maya Chen: Pricing for hosted is usage-based. We'll send a detailed pricing sheet but examples: different model tiers, with per-token pricing plus embedding separate. For a POC we can offer pilot credits and a short term cap to protect spend.

[11:02] Laura Kim: For the POC we want to run 1k messages/day light traffic for two weeks; what should we expect?
[11:08] Maya Chen: We'll estimate with your sample prompts — Samir can run the benchmark and share numbers. We can also set alerts if spend approaches a cap.

[11:20] Samir Patel: Quick note on error semantics: 4xx are client issues; 429 is rate-limit — client should backoff; 503/5xx transient — retry with exponential backoff. We return structured error payloads with error.code and error.request_id to help correlate logs.

[11:44] Amy Ross: Do you support function-calling or structured outputs?
[11:47] Samir Patel: Yes, we support function/tool calling in the chat surface. You can define schemas and the model will return structured JSON-like responses. We also support post-processing hooks in the pipeline.

[12:12] Laura Kim: Is there an example of a reconnect pattern for streaming combined with function-calling? If the stream drops mid-toolcall, we need deterministic behavior.
[12:20] Samir Patel: Pattern is: store invocation context + idempotency key, on reconnect pass last confirmed tool-call state and expect the model to either continue or return a no-op. We'll share sample code; it's a bit project-specific.

[12:44] Samir Patel: Now quick look at Optimize suggestions — console shows recommendations: lower batch size during spikes, enable KV caching for repeated prefixes (cache hit rate increased 12% in sample), and quantization profile suggestion if you want cheaper throughput.
[12:59] Ben Torres: KV caching — is that prefix cache and does it store intermediate logits?
[13:04] Samir Patel: It's prefix/KV cache; we cache internal KV tensors at the runtime layer to avoid recomputing repeated prefixes. No raw logits stored in logs; caching is internal to the runtime.

[13:22] Maya Chen: We'll attach docs for Optimize and a quick start guide for caching and batching.

[13:30] [13:35] Short pause, background noise

Topic: Private & Dedicated path briefly
[13:45] Laura Kim: If we outgrow hosted, how's migration to dedicated or private?
[13:49] Maya Chen: Same API surface. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stronger throughput SLAs; private gives VPC/on-prem options and KMS integration. Migration is mostly config and model pinning; our infra team helps the migration.

[14:05] Jason Li: For Private, do you support in-country data residency and HSM?
[14:10] Maya Chen: Yes, Private supports customer-managed networking and can integrate with HSM for key wrapping. We'll include the architecture doc in the security pack.

[14:25] Samir Patel: Back to streaming — one implementation caveat: browser SSE vs websocket differences; SSE is single-direction and easier to integrate, websockets can be used if you need bi-directional low-latency features.

[14:40] Amy Ross: For the SDKs, are they open-source? Can we look at the code?
[14:44] Maya Chen: Yes, our SDKs are open-source on GitHub. We'll share links in follow-up.

[14:52] Samir Patel: Live Q&A — latency tuning tips: 1) reduce context size, 2) pre-tokenize and cache common prefixes, 3) use lite model variants for short-turn, 4) tune batching thresholds and client-side smoothing.

[15:12] Ben Torres: For session-based usage, do you recommend storing conversation history server-side or just pass last N messages?

[15:18] Samir Patel: We usually pass a sliding window of last N messages plus an indexed summary; store full transcripts server-side if you need for analytics, but for model context keep to the most relevant subset to control tokens.

[15:34] Laura Kim: Any gotchas for token accounting we should watch?

[15:38] Maya Chen: Watch for system messages and metadata included in the request, they consume tokens; also embeddings and function-calls may add hidden tokens. Use the token_count in response for reconciliation.

[15:52] Amy Ross: Ok let's talk POC timing and owners.

[15:55] Maya Chen: Proposed: POC kickoff 12/16, run 1k-message benchmark 12/16-12/20, results and meeting on 12/21. Pilot config: hosted API in EU region, sample prompts from Ben, streaming enabled, include retry/backoff test.

[16:13] Ben Torres: Sounds good. I'll drop a sample prompt set by 12/12.

[16:18] Maya Chen: Action items recap — we'll send pricing and security docs, Samir will share demo snippet and replay, Ben will share prompts.

[16:28] Laura Kim: One last question — do you have a recommended default retry/backoff that you ship? We want to standardize.

[16:33] Samir Patel: Default SDK policy: 3 retries, base 200ms, exponential backoff with jitter capped at 3s. For rate-limits we prefer a 429-specific backoff (linear increase + jitter). We'll include config examples in the repo.

[16:50] Amy Ross: Great. That answers most of it.

[16:55] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow-up quickly.

[17:00] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: KV cache sometimes transcribed as KV cash; sample code typos in the live demo were corrected in notes. References shared: deck (link: https://redwood.ai/decks/hosted-demo), security pack (link: https://redwood.ai/security/pioneer-pack), benchmark sheet (link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/pioneer-analytics).
